## The idea

Move seven semitones upward from C and you reach G. Repeat that operation modulo
twelve and the path visits every pitch class before it returns to C. The familiar
*circle of fifths* is a picture of this compact generator, but its musical value
comes from what the order places next to what.

Neighbouring major keys share six of their seven pitch classes. C major and G
major differ only in the choice between F and F-sharp; G and D differ only at C
and C-sharp. Adjacency on the circle therefore represents a close relationship,
not decorative geometry. The same ordering tracks the growth of key signatures
and places each major key near its relative minor, three semitones below.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :piano

define :major_pitch_classes do |root|
  [0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11].map { |offset| (root + offset) % 12 }
end

circle = 12.times.map { |index| (index * 7) % 12 }
names = [:c, :g, :d, :a, :e, :b, :fs, :cs, :gs, :ds, :as, :f]

circle.each_with_index do |pitch_class, index|
  next_class = circle[(index + 1) % circle.length]
  shared = major_pitch_classes(pitch_class) & major_pitch_classes(next_class)
  relative_minor = (pitch_class - 3) % 12
  puts "#{names[index]} pc=#{pitch_class} relative_minor=#{relative_minor} shared=#{shared.length}"

  play_chord major_pitch_classes(pitch_class).first(3).map { |pc| pc + 60 },
    release: 0.65, amp: 0.7
  sleep 1
end
```

The root sequence advances by perfect fifth while the rendered three-note scale
fragments mark the long return to C. In the log, every neighbouring pair reports six shared
pitch classes. The integers remain tidy near the far side of the circle, but
their spelling does not: pitch class 6 cannot decide whether the context calls
for F-sharp or G-flat. The parallel `names` array preserves that distinct
notational decision.

## Change one thing

1. Change `7` to `5` in the generator. Five semitones upward is a fourth, which
   reverses the fifths journey while visiting the same pitch classes. Compare
   the printed order before listening for a new collection.
2. Print the set difference as well as the intersection for neighbouring
   scales. Moving clockwise replaces degree 4 of the old key with the new key's
   leading tone. Play those two notes before each fragment so the six-note overlap
   does not hide the single decisive change.
3. Move the rendered scale fragments down an octave. None of the pitch classes or
   adjacency results changes, but the cycle acquires more weight in the lower
   register. This keeps structure and voicing from becoming the same question.

## Why it works

Seven and twelve are coprime, so repeated addition of seven modulo twelve visits
all twelve residues before repeating. A step that shares a factor with twelve
closes the cycle early. Add six, for example, and the generator can only alternate
between two pitch classes. The full circle is therefore a consequence of the
relationship between the step and the size of the pitch-class space.

A major scale is generated too. Transpose `[0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11]` by seven and
reduce modulo twelve: only one member changes. That large overlap explains why
adjacent keys can provide a smooth route for modulation. It also produces the
order of sharps. Each clockwise move retains six notes and raises the remaining
degree to form the new key's leading tone.

Relative minor uses another small transformation, `(root - 3) % 12`. A relative
major and minor share their pitch collection and key signature, although they
organise those notes around different tonics. The resulting integer identifies
a pitch class, but it cannot select an enharmonic spelling. As in Lesson 10, the
system still needs a named field when F-sharp and G-flat have different musical
meanings.

The playback code deliberately renders a rough object: the first three sorted
pitch classes, lifted into one register. That is not guaranteed to be a faithful
root-position triad because a modular set has forgotten octave order. For a
harmonic renderer, rebuild the scale above its current root before selecting
degrees 1, 3, and 5. Here the crude voicing keeps attention on intersection and
adjacency, the structures the example is meant to expose.

## Take it further

Write `key_record(index)` for circle positions `-7` through `7`. Each record
should contain tonic spelling, accidental count and type, relative-minor
spelling, and the two neighbouring keys. Derive those values from circle
position instead of copying a fifteen-row table. Print the run from seven flats
through seven sharps, then play each tonic triad in the same order. When spelling
and playback disagree, inspect the representation before adjusting the synth.
